Kept for the Miami at Seek's village on Eel River in 1826, then ceded in the 1838 treaty at the Forks of the Wabash.

Ceded by the Stockbridge and Munsee on Lake Winnebago in 1839, the east half of their tract.

Granted to the Wyandot at Upper Sandusky, Ohio, in 1817 and enlarged in 1818; what remained was ceded in the 1842 treaty.
Set aside for the Wyandot on the Huron River in Michigan in 1818, then ceded in the 1842 treaty.

Ceded by the Potawatomi, Chippewa and Ottawa in 1846, the Osage River tract in Kansas.
Assigned to the Winnebago in 1832 as the Neutral Ground west of the Mississippi, partly given up in 1837, and wholly ceded in 1846.
Ceded by the Chippewa of the Mississippi and Lake Superior in 1847, the Crow Wing to Long Prairie tract in Minnesota, later given to the Winnebago.
Ceded by the Pillager band of Chippewa in 1847, land in Minnesota.
Ceded by the four Pawnee bands in 1848, land on the Platte River near Fort Childs, Nebraska.
Ceded by the Menominee in 1848, all their lands in Wisconsin; they were to receive land in Minnesota, which they refused.
Set apart for the Stockbridge as 72 sections in Minnesota by the 1848 treaty, then ceded back in 1856.
Set aside as a reservation between the Merced and Tuolumne rivers for the A-pang-asse, Aplache and other bands by an 1851 treaty that was never ratified; not a cession.
Land the A-pang-asse, Aplache and other bands were to give up outside their reserve under a March 1851 treaty that was never ratified; the 1899 federal record lists it as a cession.
Set aside as a reservation between the Chowchilla and Cah-wia rivers for the Chook-cha-nee, Chow-chil-lie and other bands by an 1851 treaty that was never ratified; not a cession.

Set aside as a reservation on King's River for the Ko-ya-te, Wack-sa-che and other bands by an 1851 treaty that was never ratified; not a cession.

Set aside as a reservation on the Stanislaus River for the Chap-pah-sim, We-chil-la and other bands by an 1851 treaty that was never ratified; not a cession.
Land outside the reserve that the Chap-pah-sim, We-chil-la and other bands were to give up under a May 1851 treaty that was never ratified.
Set aside as a reservation between Tulare and Buena Vista lakes for the Chu-nute and Wo-wol by an 1851 treaty that was never ratified; not a cession.
Set aside as a reservation near the Tule River and Paint Creek for the Yo-lum-ne and Co-ye-tie by an 1851 treaty that was never ratified; not a cession.
Land outside the reserves that the Chu-nute, Wo-wol, Yo-lum-ne and Co-ye-tie were to give up under a June 1851 treaty that was never ratified.
Set aside as a reservation between Tejon Pass and the Kern River for the Te-jon, Uva and other bands by an 1851 treaty that was never ratified; not a cession.
Land outside the reserve that the Te-jon, Uva and other bands were to give up under a June 1851 treaty that was never ratified.
Set aside as a reservation between the Bear and Yuba rivers for the Ya-cum-na, Nem-shaw and other bands by an 1851 treaty that was never ratified; not a cession.
Land outside the reserve that the Ya-cum-na, Nem-shaw and other bands were to give up under a July 1851 treaty that was never ratified.
Ceded by the Sisseton and Wahpeton Sioux in July 1851, their lands in Iowa and eastern Minnesota; in the August 1851 Mendota treaty the Medewakanton and Wahpekuta ceded the same lands.
Set aside as a reservation on the Feather River for the Mi-chop-da, Es-ki-un and other bands by an 1851 treaty that was never ratified; not a cession.
Land outside the reserve that the Mi-chop-da, Es-ki-un and other bands were to give up under an August 1851 treaty that was never ratified.

Set aside as a reservation on Clear Lake for the Ca-la-na-po, Ha-bi-na-po and other bands by an 1851 treaty that was never ratified; not a cession.
Land outside the Clear Lake reserve that the Ca-la-na-po, Ha-bi-na-po and other bands were to give up under an August 1851 treaty that was never ratified.
Land the Po-mo, Yu-ki-as and other bands were to give up, moving to the Clear Lake reserve, under an August 1851 treaty that was never ratified.
Set aside as a reservation on the Sacramento River for the Co-lu, Wil-lay and other bands by an 1851 treaty that was never ratified; not a cession.
Land outside the reserve that the Co-lu, Wil-lay and other bands were to give up under a September 1851 treaty that was never ratified.

Recognized by the 1851 Fort Laramie treaty as territory of the northern Plains nations, including the Sioux, Gros Ventre, Mandan, Arikara, Assiniboin, Crow, Cheyenne and Arapaho; not a cession or reservation.
Set aside as a reservation on the Cosumnes River for the Cu-lee, Wo-pum-ne and other bands by an 1851 treaty that was never ratified; not a cession.
Land outside the reserve that the Cu-lee, Wo-pum-ne and other bands were to give up under a September 1851 treaty that was never ratified.
Set aside as a reservation on the Klamath River for the Hoo-pah (Trinity River), Peh-tuck (Upper Klamath) and Poh-lik (Lower Klamath) by an 1851 treaty that was never ratified; not a cession.
Land outside the Klamath River reserve that the Hoo-pah, Peh-tuck and Poh-lik were to give up under an October 1851 treaty that was never ratified.
Set aside as a reservation on the upper Klamath River for the I-ka-ruck, Ko-se-tah and other bands by an 1851 treaty that was never ratified; not a cession.
Land outside the reserve that the I-ka-ruck, Ko-se-tah and other bands were to give up under a November 1851 treaty that was never ratified.

Set aside as a reservation on California's southern line for the Diegueño by an 1852 treaty at Santa Isabel that was never ratified; not a cession.
Land outside the reserve that the Diegueño were to give up under an 1852 treaty at Santa Isabel that was never ratified.
Set aside in 1853 by Superintendent Beale, not by treaty, as the Tejon Pass reserve for the Tejon and San Imirio; not a cession. It was later reduced and abandoned.
Ceded by the Rogue River Indians in the 1853 Treaty of Table Rock, land in Oregon and California, while they kept a temporary reserve.
Ceded by the Cow Creek band of Umpqua in 1853, land in Oregon, while they kept a temporary reserve.
Ceded by the Oto and Missouri in 1854, all their country west of the Missouri River in Nebraska, except a reserve they kept on the Big Blue River.
Ceded by the Omaha in 1854, their lands south of a line near the Ayoway River in Nebraska; they kept land north of it.
Ceded by the Delaware in 1854, their lands in Kansas, except land sold to the Wyandot and a reserve they kept.
Inside the 1854 Delaware cession, four sections were confirmed to the Christian (Munsee) Indians, who sold them in 1857; Congress confirmed the sale in 1858.
Given to the Shawnee of Missouri as Kansas land in 1825, then ceded in the 1854 treaty, except 200,000 acres granted back to them.
Given to the Shawnee of Missouri as Kansas land in 1825 and ceded in 1854; this part was set aside for allotments to absent Shawnee and later sold to settlers.
Assigned to the Menominee in Minnesota by the 1848 treaty; they refused to move there and gave it up in 1854 in return for a reserve on the Wolf River in Wisconsin.
Given to the Menominee in 1854 as a home on the Wolf River in Wisconsin, in exchange for giving up their Minnesota tract; not a cession.
Assigned in 1836 to the Iowa and the Sauk and Fox of the Missouri; the Iowa ceded their share in 1854, and the Sauk and Fox of the Missouri ceded theirs the next day.
Assigned in 1836 as the lower half of a strip for the Sauk and Fox of the Missouri, then ceded by them in 1854.
Assigned to the Kickapoo in Kansas by 1832 treaties; this is the part they ceded in 1854, while keeping a reserve.
Assigned in Kansas to the Kaskaskia, Peoria, Piankishaw and Wea in 1832; this is the part they ceded in the 1854 treaty.
Assigned in Kansas to the Kaskaskia, Peoria, Piankishaw and Wea in 1832; the 1854 treaty kept 10 sections as a shared reserve, which the 1867 treaty ceded and sold to settlers.
Promised to the Miami in Kansas in 1838 and assigned in 1840, then ceded in the 1854 treaty, except a 70,000-acre reserve.
Kept by the Miami as a 70,000-acre home in Kansas under the 1854 treaty and partly divided into allotments; an act of March 1873 provided for selling the rest.
Set aside in 1854 by Superintendent Henley, not by treaty, as the Nome Lackee reserve for the Nome Lackee, Nome Cult and Nir-muck; not a cession, and later abandoned.
Ceded by the Chippewa of Lake Superior and the Mississippi in the 1854 Treaty of La Pointe, their lands in Minnesota.
Set apart for the L'Anse and Vieux Desert bands of Chippewa in Michigan by the 1854 La Pointe treaty; a reservation, not a cession.
Set apart for the La Pointe band of Chippewa (Bad River) in Wisconsin by the 1854 La Pointe treaty; a reservation, not a cession.
Set apart for the La Pointe band of Chippewa (Bad River and Madeline Island) by the 1854 La Pointe treaty; the Secretary of the Interior approved the land chosen in 1859. Never ceded.
Set apart for Wisconsin bands of Chippewa near Lac du Flambeau by the 1854 La Pointe treaty; a reservation, not a cession.
Promised to the Chippewa at Lac Court Oreilles by the 1854 La Pointe treaty; the land chosen was approved in 1873 and the rest of the held land reopened for sale. The reserve was never ceded.
Set apart for the Fond du Lac bands of Chippewa in Minnesota in 1854, then ceded in an agreement signed in November 1889 under the Nelson Act.
Set apart for the Grand Portage band of Chippewa in Minnesota in 1854, then ceded in an agreement signed in October 1889.

Ceded by the Calapooia and allied bands of the Willamette Valley in the 1855 Treaty of Dayton, land in Oregon.
Ceded by the Sklallam in the 1855 Treaty of Point No Point, land in Washington.
Set apart as six sections at the head of Hood Canal for the Sklallam by the 1855 Point No Point treaty; a reservation, not a cession.

Set apart for the Makah by the 1855 Treaty of Neah Bay; a reservation, not a cession.
Ceded by the Chippewa of the Mississippi in 1855, land in Minnesota.
Set apart at Leech Lake for the Pillager and Lake Winnibigoshish bands by the 1855 treaty, and later enlarged by executive orders; not a cession.
Set apart at Lake Winnibigoshish for the Pillager and Lake Winnibigoshish bands by the 1855 treaty; a reservation, not a cession.
Set apart at Cass Lake for the Pillager and Lake Winnibigoshish bands by the 1855 treaty; a reservation, not a cession.

Ceded by the Walla-walla, Cayuse and Umatilla in the 1855 Treaty of Walla Walla, land in Oregon and Washington.
Kept by the Walla-walla, Cayuse and Umatilla as the Umatilla reservation in the 1855 treaty; not a cession.
Ceded by the Yakima and allied tribes in the 1855 Yakama treaty, land in Washington.
Kept by the Yakima as their reservation in the 1855 Yakama treaty; not a cession.

Ceded by the Confederated Tribes of Middle Oregon in the 1855 Warm Springs treaty, while they kept a reserve.
Kept by the Confederated Tribes of Middle Oregon as the Warm Springs reserve in the 1855 treaty; an 1894 executive order only fixed its northern boundary. Never ceded.

Set aside in 1855 by executive order as a 25,000-acre reserve on the Klamath River for the Klamath, joined to the Hoopa reservation in 1891, and returned to the public domain, with allotments, by an 1892 act.
Ceded by the Molalla in the 1855 treaty at Dayton, land in Oregon.
Set up informally in 1856 as the Tule River (Madden Farm) reservation in California; not a cession, and later abandoned.
Part of the Menominee's 1854 Wolf River home; two townships in its southwest corner were ceded in 1856 for the Stockbridge and Munsee, and an 1871 act ordered all but 18 sections sold.
Reserves for the Niskwali and neighbors (Puyallup, Nisqually, Muckleshoot) resized and moved by executive order in January 1857, as the treaty allowed; not a cession.
Set up as the Grand Ronde reservation for the Confederated Bands of the Willamette Valley by executive order in June 1857, following the 1855 treaty; not a cession.

Kept for the Yankton Sioux's use as the Red Pipestone quarry in Minnesota by the 1858 treaty; not a cession.
Kept by the Medewakanton and Wahpekute Sioux in 1858 as a reserve south of the Minnesota River, with the north-side portion left for the Senate to decide; not a cession.
Set apart by an 1859 act of Congress as the Gila River reservation for the Pima and Maricopa, on land they already lived on; not a cession.
Granted to the Winnebago in 1855 as 18 miles square on the Blue Earth River in Minnesota; the western part was given up in 1859, to be sold by the United States on their behalf.
Furnished in 1836 to the Swan Creek and Black River Chippewa as land in Kansas; apart from a small home tract, it was sold by the United States on their behalf under the 1859 treaty.
Assigned to the Sauk and Fox of the Mississippi in Kansas in 1842; this part was given up in 1859, to be sold on their behalf, and an 1867 treaty disposed of what remained unsold.
Chosen for the Kansa after their 1846 cession and cut down in 1859; this is the part they kept, later sold under acts of 1872 to 1880.
Chosen for the Kansa after their 1846 cession; the part beyond what they kept was given up in 1859, to be sold by the United States on their behalf.
Set apart in 1859 by agent Jarvis, not by treaty, as a reserve at Ruby Valley, Nevada, for the Western Shoshoni; not a cession.
Set aside by officials, not by treaty, as the Fresno River reservation for the Chow-chilla, Chook-chan-cie and Poho-neche; reported abandoned in 1859.
Chosen by an agent and approved by the Commissioner of Indian Affairs in 1860 as the Gila Apache reservation in New Mexico; not a cession.
Kept by the Delaware as a Kansas reserve when they ceded land in 1854; the 1860 treaty divided part into allotments and sold the rest to a railroad, confirmed in 1861.

Defined as Cheyenne and Arapaho territory by the 1851 Fort Laramie treaty (noted in the 1899 federal record as never ratified), ceded except a reserve at Fort Wise in 1861, with more claims given up in 1865.
Chosen as a Nebraska reserve by the Sauk and Fox of the Missouri under the 1854 treaty, then ceded by them in the 1861 treaty.
Part of the 1836 strip that the Iowa kept as their home after the 1854 and 1861 treaties; an 1876 act allowed 10 sections off its west end to be sold.
Set apart for Ute bands as the Uintah Valley reserve in 1861; part was taken for a military reservation in 1887, and part returned to the public domain by an 1888 act.
The rest of the land claimed by the Uintah Uta, taken by the United States in 1861 without any formal purchase; neither a treaty cession nor a reservation.
Given to the Ottawa of Blanchard's Fork and Roche de Boeuf as a Kansas reserve in 1831; the 1862 treaty divided it into allotments and sold the rest for the tribe.
Part of the Kickapoo's Kansas reserve from 1832, left after their 1854 cession; the 1862 treaty divided it into individual allotments and sold part to a railroad, ending tribal title.
Part of the Kickapoo's Kansas reserve from 1832, left after their 1854 cession; the 1862 treaty set it apart to be held in common, and it is their present reservation.
The eastern part of the Winnebago's Blue Earth reserve, kept in 1859, was sold on their behalf under an 1863 act once they were removed.
Set apart in 1851 along the Minnesota River for the Sioux and kept south of the river in 1858; after the 1862 outbreak, an 1863 act took it and ordered it sold.
Kept by the Nez Percé as a large reserve in Idaho, Oregon and Washington in 1855, then given up in the 1863 treaty, except a smaller new reserve.
Kept by the Nez Percé as their smaller reserve in 1863; the land not allotted to individuals was ceded in a May 1893 agreement that Congress confirmed in 1894.
Set apart at Crow Creek, Dakota, for the Sioux of the Mississippi by executive order in July 1863; a reservation, not a cession.
Defined as Western Shoshoni country by the 1863 Ruby Valley treaty; the United States took it over without formal purchase. Described territory, not a cession or reservation.
Ceded by the Red Lake and Pembina Chippewa in the 1863 Old Crossing treaty, land in Minnesota and North Dakota.
Kept by the Red Lake Chippewa as unceded land under the 1863 Old Crossing treaty; a reservation they retained, not a cession.
Defined as Shoshone-Goship country by an 1863 treaty; the 1899 federal record says the United States took it over without formal purchase. Recognized territory, not a cession.
Set up in 1864 on the President's order as the Bosque Redondo reserve for the Apache in New Mexico, 40 miles square; not a cession, and later abandoned.

One of four Utah reserves for the Uta set up between 1856 and 1859 (probably the Spanish Fork reserve); an 1864 act provided for vacating and selling them, and an 1878 act returned them to the public domain.

One of four Utah reserves for the Uta set up between 1856 and 1859 (probably the Corn Creek reserve); an 1864 act provided for vacating and selling them, and an 1878 act returned them to the public domain.

One of four Utah reserves for the Uta set up between 1856 and 1859 (probably the San Pete reserve); an 1864 act provided for vacating and selling them, and an 1878 act returned them to the public domain.

One of four Utah reserves for the Uta set up between 1856 and 1859 (probably the Deep Creek reserve); an 1864 act provided for vacating and selling them, and an 1878 act returned them to the public domain.
Set aside for the Chippewa of the Mississippi as the Gull Lake reserve by the 1855 treaty, then ceded in the 1864 treaty.
Set aside for the Chippewa of the Mississippi as the Mille Lac reserve in 1855, ceded with conditions in 1864, and their right to live there given up in an 1889 agreement.
Set aside for the Chippewa of the Mississippi as the Sandy Lake reserve by the 1855 treaty, then ceded in the 1864 treaty.
Set aside for the Chippewa of the Mississippi as the Rabbit Lake reserve by the 1855 treaty, then ceded in the 1864 treaty.
Set aside for the Chippewa of the Mississippi as the Pokagomin Lake reserve by the 1855 treaty, then ceded in the 1864 treaty.
Land of the Chehalis, Chinook, Klatsop and Klikitat in Washington, taken by the United States without any treaty; neither a cession nor a reservation.
Approved by the Secretary of the Interior in 1864 as a reserve for the Chehalis and others; not a cession.
Ordered in 1864 by the President as a mill and timber reserve on the Truckee River for the Paiute of Pyramid Lake; a reservation, not a cession, later quietly abandoned.
Chosen in 1864 by Superintendent Wiley as the Hoopa Valley reserve for the Hupa, given set boundaries by executive order in 1876, and extended along the Klamath River in 1891. Never ceded.
Ceded by the Klamath, Modok and Yahooskin band of Snake Indians in the 1864 Klamath Lake treaty, land in Oregon and California.
Kept by the Klamath, Modok and Yahooskin band of Snake Indians as the Klamath reservation in the 1864 treaty; not a cession.
Enlarged in 1864 by the Secretary of the Interior, the Port Madison reserve set up for the Dwamish by the 1855 treaty; a reservation, not a cession.
Set up by an 1865 act of Congress as the Colorado River reservation in Arizona and enlarged by executive order in 1874. Never ceded.
Kept by the Omaha as their Nebraska reserve in 1854; a strip off its north side was ceded in 1865 so the Winnebago could be settled there.
Set up for the Winnebago at Crow Creek, Dakota, under an 1863 act and a July 1863 executive order, then ceded back in the March 1865 treaty.
Given to the Winnebago in 1865 as a home in Nebraska, on land the Omaha had ceded that month; a reservation, not a cession by them.
Washo country, taken over by settlers between 1855 and 1865 without any purchase; an 1865 order for two small reserves was never carried out. Neither a cession nor a reservation.
Ceded by the Woll-pah-pe tribe of Snake Indians in August 1865 at Sprague River Valley, Oregon; this area is the part of that cession that does not overlap others.
Kept for the Osage as a Kansas reserve within their 1825 cession, then ceded and sold under the 1865 treaty and a later act of July 1870.
Ceded by the Osage in the 1865 Canville treaty, a 20-mile-wide strip off the north side of their Kansas reservation, to be sold by the United States on their behalf.
Recognized as Cheyenne and Arapaho territory in 1851, made their reserve at Fort Wise in 1861, and ceded in the 1865 Little Arkansas treaty.
Set apart as a reservation for the Comanche and Kiowa by the October 1865 treaty; not a cession. Part of the rest was returned to the public domain by an 1875 act.
Set aside as the Coast (Siletz) reserve for Indians of the Oregon coast by executive order in 1855, reduced in 1865, and the unallotted rest ceded in an 1892 agreement confirmed in 1894.
Given by the Creek to the Seminole in 1856, then ceded by the Seminole to the United States in the March 1866 treaty.
Granted to the Seminole in 1866 as a reserve from the western half of the Creek lands in Indian Territory; not a cession by them.
Set apart near Nett Lake for the Bois Forte band of Chippewa under the 1866 treaty, according to the 1899 federal record's remarks; not a cession.
Promised to the Bois Forte band of Chippewa in the 1866 treaty as a reserve of at least 100,000 acres (Nett Lake area), then ceded in a November 1889 agreement.
Promised to the Bois Forte band of Chippewa in 1866, set apart as the Deer Creek reserve by the President in 1883, and ceded in a November 1889 agreement.
Leased by the Choctaw and Chickasaw in 1855, their country west of the 98th meridian, for settling other tribes; they ceded this 'leased district' in the 1866 treaty.
Kept by the Delaware as their Kansas reserve in 1854, partly sold in 1860, and the rest sold to the Missouri River Railroad Company in the 1866 treaty.
The Cherokee Outlet: guaranteed to the Cherokee in 1833, left with them in 1866 with a United States right to settle friendly Indians there, and ceded in an 1891 agreement confirmed in 1893.
The Cherokee Neutral Land in Kansas: granted to the Cherokee in the 1835 New Echota treaty, given up in 1866 to be sold on their behalf, with an 1868 treaty reaffirming its sale to James F. Joy.
The Cherokee Strip in Kansas, given up by the Cherokee in 1866 to be sold on their behalf; an 1877 act provided for selling the unsold part at a lower price.
Guaranteed to the Cherokee in Indian Territory by the 1833 treaty and kept by them as their home in the 1866 treaty; the 1899 federal record lists no cession of this area.
Set apart as a reservation at Shoalwater Bay, Washington, by executive order in September 1866; not a cession.
Assigned to the Sauk and Fox of the Mississippi in Kansas in 1842, reduced to a smaller reserve in 1859, and the unsold rest ceded in the 1867 treaty.
Provided to the Sauk and Fox of the Mississippi in 1867 as a 750-square-mile reservation in Indian Territory, then ceded in an agreement Congress confirmed in February 1891.
Set apart at Lake Traverse for the Sisseton and Wahpeton Sioux by the 1867 treaty; the land not allotted to individuals was ceded in an agreement Congress confirmed in March 1891.
Set apart at Devil's Lake for the Sisseton and Wahpeton Sioux by the 1867 treaty; a reservation, not a cession.
Granted to the Seneka in 1832; in the 1867 treaty they ceded this strip off its north side, which was then set apart as the Wyandot's home.
Granted to the Seneka in Indian Territory in 1832 and kept as their home in 1867 after they ceded a strip; an 1889 act only provided for allotments, and no cession is recorded.
Part of the 1832 grant to the mixed Seneka and Shawnee; the Seneka ceded the north half in 1867, and it was granted to the Peoria, Kaskaskia, Piankishaw and Wea.
Part of the 1832 Seneka and Shawnee grant; the Shawnee ceded these 12,000 acres in 1867, and the United States sold them to the Ottawa as their home.
Ceded in an 1867 treaty in which the Seneka, Shawnee and Quapaw gave up strips of their Indian Territory reserves, later assigned to the Wyandot, Ottawa and others.
A half-mile strip in Kansas off the north line of the Quapaw's 150-section reserve, granted in 1833, ceded by the Quapaw in the 1867 treaty.
The west end of the Quapaw reserve granted in 1833, ceded by the Quapaw in 1867 and granted to the Peoria and associated tribes.
The rest of the Quapaw's 150-section reserve granted in 1833, kept by the Quapaw as their home in 1867; the 1899 federal record lists no cession.
Set apart for the Potawatomi in Indian Territory as a 30-mile-square tract in 1867 and shared with the Absentee Shawnee from 1872; ceded in agreements Congress confirmed in March 1891.
Ceded by the Chippewa of the Mississippi in March 1867, the lands secured to them by the 1864 treaty, except a part they kept.
Kept by the Chippewa of the Mississippi as a reservation under the March 1867 treaty; not a cession.
Set apart as the White Earth reservation, 36 townships including White Earth and Rice lakes, for the Chippewa of the Mississippi by the March 1867 treaty; not a cession.
Part of the 1865 Comanche and Kiowa reserve that they gave up in the 1867 Medicine Lodge treaty, keeping only a smaller reservation, which the Apache agreed to share.
Set apart for the Comanche and Kiowa by the 1865 treaty, then cut back to a smaller reservation by the 1867 Medicine Lodge treaty, which gave up the rest.
Set apart in 1854, with the Texas legislature's permission, as one of two reservations on the Brazos for the Comanche and other Texas Indians; abandoned in 1859. Not a cession.
Set apart in 1854, with the Texas legislature's permission, as the second of two reservations on the Brazos for the Comanche and other Texas Indians; abandoned in 1859. Not a cession.
Added to the Santee Sioux's Niobrara reserve in Nebraska by executive order in November 1867; not a cession, and later changed.
Given up by the Uta bands in the March 1868 treaty, which gave up all claim to their land outside the new reservation, in Colorado and Utah.
Recognized as Crow country by the 1851 Fort Laramie treaty (noted in the 1899 federal record as never ratified); the Crow gave up this land outside their reserve in the 1868 treaty.
Set apart as the Navaho reservation by the June 1868 treaty; not a cession, and later enlarged by executive orders.
Given up by the Navaho in the June 1868 treaty, which gave up their right to land beyond the new reservation, in New Mexico, Utah and Arizona.
Given up by the Shoshoni and Bannock in the July 1868 Fort Bridger treaty, which gave up their right to all land outside their reservation.
The Smith River reservation in California, closed by Congress in July 1868, which moved the Indians living there; the closing of a reservation, not a cession by a tribe.
Set apart as the Mendocino Indian Reservation in California by executive order in 1856, then returned to the public domain by Congress in 1868.
Set aside for the Santee Sioux between the Big Sioux and James rivers by executive order in 1867, never occupied, and returned to the public domain in 1869.

Set up as the Fort Hall reserve in Idaho by executive orders of 1867 and 1869 under the 1868 treaty; only 1,840 acres for railroads were given up (1888), and an 1889 Lemhi cession was never carried out.
Set apart for the Cheyenne and Arapaho on the North Fork of the Canadian River by executive order in 1869, then ceded, subject to allotments, in an agreement Congress confirmed in March 1891.

Taken from the Santee Sioux's Niobrara reservation in Nebraska in August 1869, when an executive order returned this part to the public domain; a taking by the United States, not a return to the tribe.
Set apart for the San Pasqual and Pala Valley Mission Indians by executive order in January 1870; not a cession. Trouble with settlers led to its abandonment in 1871.
The second part of the reserve set apart for the San Pasqual and Pala Valley Mission Indians by executive order in January 1870; not a cession, and abandoned in 1871.
Recognized as Arikara, Gros Ventre and Mandan land by the 1851 Fort Laramie treaty; by accepting the Fort Berthold reserve in 1870, they were treated as giving up this land outside it.
Approved as the Tularosa River reservation for the Southern Apache in 1871, then returned to the public domain by executive order in 1874.
Claimed by the Methow, Okanagan and other tribes and taken by the United States without any treaty; the 1899 federal record lists no cession, only reservations made by executive order.
Set apart as the Colville reservation by executive order in April 1872, then returned to the public domain in July 1872 and replaced by a different tract.
Provided for by Congress in 1870 as an Osage reservation in Indian Territory, chosen in 1871, and its boundaries confirmed by an 1872 act; no cession is recorded.
Confirmed by Congress in June 1872 as the Kansa reserve in Indian Territory; not a cession.
Set apart by executive order in July 1872 in place of the April 1872 tract, which was returned to the public domain; this is the present Colville reservation. Not a cession.
Withdrawn in Oregon in 1871 so a Malheur reservation could be chosen from it; the rest was returned to the public domain in 1872.
Defined as land claimed by the Sisseton and Wahpeton Sioux in 1867; the part outside their reserves was ceded in a September 1872 agreement that Congress ratified in 1873 and 1874.
The southern part of the Wind River reservation set apart for the Shoshones in 1868, ceded in a September 1872 agreement that Congress ratified in 1874.
Set apart as the Shoshoni's Wind River reservation in 1868 and kept after they ceded the southern part in 1872; a small military reservation for Fort Washakie was carved out in 1887.
Set apart for the Wichita and allied bands in Indian Territory by an October 1872 agreement that was never ratified; not a cession, though the agreement also claimed to give up lands elsewhere.
Approved as the Camp Grant reservation for the Apache in 1871, then returned to the public domain by executive order in 1872.
Set by an 1873 act as the place the Pembina Chippewa would be moved to on the White Earth reservation, with a township chosen in 1883; a reservation assignment, not a cession.
Bought by the United States from the Creek for the Seminole under an 1873 act, 175,000 acres east of the earlier Creek-Seminole line.
Taken from the Round Valley reservation in California when an 1873 act returned this southern part to the public domain.
Set apart in the Wallowa Valley for the Nez Percé by executive order in 1873, then returned to the public domain in 1875.
Taken from the San Carlos division of the White Mountain Apache reservation when an August 1873 executive order returned this part to the public domain.
Set up as the Tule River reserve for the Tule River, King's River and Owen's River Indians by executive order in October 1873, replacing a January 1873 order; not a cession.
Added to the Makah reservation by executive order in October 1873; not a cession, and part of the present Makah reservation.
Added to the Lake Winnibigoshish reservation by executive order in October 1873, from land the Chippewa had ceded in 1867; not a cession.
Added to the Leech Lake reservation by executive order in November 1873, from land ceded in 1867; not a cession.
Promised to the Quinaielt and Quillehute as a reserve in the 1855 treaty and enlarged by executive order in 1873; the reservation was never ceded.
Set up as the Coeur d'Alène reservation in Idaho by an 1867 order, replaced in 1873; only small parts were later given up (an 1892 act and an 1894 agreement), and the reservation remains.
Claimed by the Coeur d'Alène outside their reservation in Idaho, Washington and Montana; treated as given up when they accepted the 1873 reserve, and formally ceded in an agreement confirmed in 1891.
Added to the Colorado River reservation by executive order in 1873 and enlarged again in 1874; never ceded.
Added to the Lummi reserve in Washington by executive order in November 1873; not a cession.
Fixed as the Santee Sioux's Niobrara reserve in Nebraska by executive orders through 1873; land not allotted to individuals was returned to the public domain in 1885.
Set apart for the Crow in the Judith Basin by executive order in 1874, under an 1873 agreement Congress never ratified, then returned to the public domain in 1875.
Added to the Skokomish reservation on Hood Canal for the Sklallam by executive order in February 1874; not a cession.
Set up as the Walker River reservation for the Paiute by executive order in March 1874; it had been recommended in 1859 and surveyed in 1864. Not a cession.
Set up as the Pyramid Lake reservation for the Paiute by executive order in March 1874; not a cession.
Paiute country in California and Nevada, taken over by the United States without any formal giving up of the land by the Paiute.
Set apart on the San Juan River for the Jicarilla Apache by executive order in 1874, under an agreement Congress never approved, then canceled in 1876.
Set up as the Muckleshoot reservation by executive order in 1857 and added to by a second order in 1874; never ceded.
Part of the land recognized as Blackfoot territory in 1855 that became a shared reserve for the Gros Ventre, Piegan, Blood, Blackfoot and River Crow (1873 order, fixed by an 1874 act); not ceded.
Set apart as part of the Uta reservation by the 1868 treaty, then ceded in a September 1873 agreement ratified in April 1874; a 4-mile-square tract in the Uncompahgre Valley was kept in 1876.
Added to the Leech Lake reservation by executive order in May 1874, from land ceded in 1867; not a cession.
Added to the Lake Winnibigoshish reservation by executive order in May 1874, from land ceded in 1867; not a cession.
Paid for by an 1874 act: land of the L'Anse and Vieux Desert Chippewa east of Huron Bay, Michigan, outside their reservation; a purchase treated as a cession.
Part of the reservation the Omaha kept in 1854, bought for the Winnebago under a June 1874 act; the deed, for 12,347.55 acres, was signed in July 1874.
Ceded by the Eastern Shawnee in a June 1874 agreement, 4,000 acres in the northeast corner of their reserve for the Modoc, confirmed by an 1875 act.
Set apart around San Xavier del Bac as a reservation for the Papago by executive order in July 1874; not a cession.
Set apart in 1871 as part of the White Mountain Apache reservation; this eastern part was returned to the public domain by executive order in 1874.
Part of the 1873 reserve for the Blackfoot, Blood, Piegan, Gros Ventre and River Crow left outside the area fixed by an 1874 act, and returned to the public domain by executive order in 1874.
Set apart on the Lemhi River for the Shoshoni, Bannock and Sheepeater by executive order in February 1875, in place of a reserve from a treaty that was never ratified; not a cession.
Set apart as the Moapa River reserve for the Paiute in 1873 and replaced in 1874; most of it was returned to the public domain in 1875, keeping only 1,000 acres.
The 1,000 acres of the Moapa River reservation kept for the Paiute in 1875, with boundaries approved that year; never ceded.
Part of the Coast (later Siletz) reservation set apart for Indians on the Oregon coast by executive order in 1855, returned to the public domain by an 1875 act.
A second part of the Coast (Siletz) reservation set apart for Indians on the Oregon coast in 1855, returned to the public domain by an 1875 act.
Secured for the Eastern Band of Cherokee under an 1875 act: the Qualla boundary and some small tracts in North Carolina, with funds used to complete their title. Not a cession.
Added to the Great Sioux reservation, north of the 46th parallel in North Dakota, by executive order in March 1875; not a cession, and later given up by executive orders.
Approved as the Camp Verde reservation for the Apache in 1871, then returned to the public domain by executive order in 1875.
The Round Valley reservation in California as fixed after an 1873 act returned its southern part to the public domain and redrew its boundaries, proclaimed in 1875; not ceded.
Part of the land the 1868 Fort Laramie treaty treated as unceded Sioux territory, with hunting rights, in Nebraska; the Sioux gave up these rights in a June 1875 agreement.
Added to the Crow reservation by executive order in 1875, then canceled in 1876.
Added to the Uta reservation by executive order in 1875, then returned to the public domain in 1882.
Given its boundaries as the Hot Springs reservation for the Southern Apache in December 1875, then returned to the public domain by executive order in 1877.
Part of the Hot Springs reserve set apart for the Southern Apache in 1874 that was left out of the December 1875 order and reopened for sale.
Added to the Malheur reservation for the Paiute and Shoshoni in 1875; part was returned to the public domain in January 1876.
Kept by the Pawnee as a reserve on the Loup Fork in Nebraska under the 1857 treaty; an 1876 act provided for selling it, with their consent, as they moved to Indian Territory.
Provided to the Pawnee as a new reservation in Indian Territory by an 1876 act, then ceded in a November 1892 agreement that Congress confirmed in March 1893.
Taken from the White Mountain Apache reservation when an April 1876 executive order returned this western part to the public domain.
Created as the Colorado River reservation by an 1865 act, enlarged by executive orders, and given corrected boundaries in 1876; never ceded.
The former Camp Wright military reserve, one square mile, added to the Round Valley Indian reservation by executive order in July 1876; not a cession.
Kept by the Oto and Missouri as a reserve on the Big Blue in 1854; an August 1876 act allowed 120,000 acres off its west end to be sold with their consent.
Added to the Gila River reservation for the Pima and Maricopa by executive order in August 1876; not a cession.
Recognized as unceded Indian territory in the 1868 Fort Laramie treaty, then ceded by the Sioux, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho in a September 1876 agreement confirmed by Congress in February 1877.
Ceded by the Sioux, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho in the September 1876 Black Hills agreement, ratified in February 1877: the part of the Great Sioux reserve west of a set line.
Added to the north end of the Sioux reserve, between the 46th parallel and the Cannon Ball River, by the September 1876 agreement; not a cession.
Set apart as the Chiricahua reservation for the Apache by executive order in 1872, then canceled in 1876.
Taken from the White Mountain Apache reservation when a January 1877 executive order returned this part to the public domain.
Taken from the White Mountain Apache reservation when a March 1877 executive order returned this part to the public domain; what remained is the reserve as it stood in the 1899 federal record.
Approved as part of the White Mountain Apache reservation in 1871, then returned to the public domain by executive order in 1877.
Set apart as the Duck Valley reservation in Nevada and Idaho for the Western Shoshoni by executive order in April 1877; not a cession.
Set apart as the Carlin Farms reservation in Nevada for the northwestern Shoshoni in 1877, then returned to the public domain in 1879.
Bought from the Cherokee for Joseph's band of Nez Percé under an 1878 act; they deeded it to the United States in 1885, and the Tonkawa ceded it in an agreement confirmed in March 1893.
Set apart as the Tule River reserve by 1873 orders; part was returned to the public domain in 1878, and the rest is the reserve as it stood in the 1899 federal record.
Added to the Navajo reservation in Arizona by executive order in October 1878; not a cession.
Promised to the Muache, Capote and Wiminuche Uta on the San Juan River in an 1878 agreement that was never ratified, set apart in 1879, and returned to the public domain in 1882.
Added to the White Earth reservation for the Chippewa of Minnesota in 1879, then canceled in 1883.
Set apart for the Pima and Maricopa on the Salt River by executive order in June 1879, replacing a January 1879 order; not a cession.
The second of two tracts set apart for the Pima and Maricopa on the Salt River by executive order in June 1879; not a cession.
Set apart in Dakota for Drifting Goose's band of Yanktonai Sioux in 1879, then returned to the public domain in 1880.
Added to the Great Sioux reservation by executive orders in 1875 and 1876, then returned to the public domain by an August 1879 executive order.
Added again to the Navaho reservation, in Arizona and New Mexico, by executive order in January 1880; not a cession.

Set apart as the Columbia reservation for Moses' band of Nez Percé by 1879 and 1880 orders, given up in a July 1883 agreement ratified in 1884, and returned to the public domain in 1886, except allotments.
Recognized as Crow land in 1851 and set apart as their reservation in 1868; this part was ceded in a June 1880 agreement confirmed in April 1882.
Recognized as Arikara, Gros Ventre and Mandan land in 1851 and set apart as part of the Fort Berthold reservation in 1870; returned to the public domain in 1880.
Set apart as the Fort Berthold reservation for the Arikara, Gros Ventre and Mandan in 1870, with an addition in 1880; this area was not ceded in the period covered.
Added in 1875 to the reserve of the Gros Ventre, Piegan, Blood, Blackfoot and River Crow; this part was returned to the public domain in 1880.
Added in 1875 to the reserve of the Gros Ventre, Piegan, Blood, Blackfoot and River Crow; this part stayed in their reserve after another part was returned to the public domain in 1880.
Set apart as a reserve for the Jicarilla Apache in 1880, then returned to the public domain in 1884.
Set apart as a reserve for the Spokane by executive order in 1881; in a March 1887 agreement, carried out by an 1892 act, they gave up their claims and moved to the Coeur d'Alène reservation.
The rest of the Oto and Missouri reserve in Kansas and Nebraska, to be sold with their consent under an 1881 act; they moved to Indian Territory.
Chosen and bought from the Cherokee as a new reserve for the Oto and Missouri in Indian Territory under an 1881 act; a reservation, not a cession.
A new reservation in Indian Territory for the Ponka, authorized in 1878 and paid for under an 1881 act with land bought from the Cherokee; not ceded.
Set apart at Vermilion Lake for the Bois Forte band of Chippewa by executive order in December 1881; not a cession.
Set apart in Utah as a reserve for the Uncompahgre Uta by executive order in January 1882; it formed their reserve in the 1899 federal record. Not a cession.
Added to the Sioux reservation from Nebraska land by executive order in 1882, and included in the Pine Ridge reservation by an 1889 act; not ceded.
Set apart for the Havasupai on the floor of Cataract Canyon by executive order in March 1882, in place of an 1880 reserve; not a cession.
Added to the Gila River reservation for the Pima and Maricopa by executive order in May 1882; not a cession.
What remained of the 1868 Crow reservation after the 1880 cession; an 1882 act only ratified a 400-foot railroad right of way.
The western part of the reservation the Omaha kept in 1854; an August 1882 act provided for selling it with their consent.
The rest of the Omaha reservation, to be divided and deeded to individuals or the tribe under an 1882 act; not ceded.
Set apart as part of the Malheur reservation in 1872 and redrawn in 1876; this southern part was returned to the public domain by a September 1882 executive order.
Set apart as the Gila Bend reserve for the Papago and others by executive order in December 1882; not a cession.
Set apart by executive order in December 1882 as a reservation for the Moki and other Indians in Arizona; not a cession.
Set apart as a reserve for the Walapai in Arizona by executive order in January 1883; not a cession.
Set apart in 1879 as the northern part of the Columbia reservation for Moses' band of Nez Percé, then returned to the public domain in February 1883.
Once part of the Fort Stanton reserves for the Mescalero Apache (1873 to 1882), but left out when a March 1883 executive order fixed the present reserve.
Set apart as the Fort Stanton reserve for the Mescalero Apache in 1873 and redrawn in 1883; not ceded.
Set apart as the Zuñi reservation by executive order in 1877, with boundaries amended in 1883; not ceded.
Set apart as the Malheur reservation in 1872, enlarged in 1875 and redrawn in 1876; a May 1883 executive order returned it to the public domain, except 320 acres.
The 320 acres of the Malheur reservation kept in 1883, the north half of the Camp Harney military reserve, then returned to the public domain in 1889.
Set apart as a reserve for the Yuma on the Arizona side in July 1883, then returned to the public domain in January 1884.
Set apart as a reserve for the Iowa in Indian Territory by executive order in August 1883; not a cession.
Authorized by acts of 1870 and 1871 and set apart in 1883 as a reserve for the Kickapoo in Indian Territory, then ceded in a September 1891 agreement confirmed in March 1893.
Added to the Pima and Maricopa reserve on the Salt River by executive order in November 1883; not a cession.
Set apart as a reserve for the Yuma on the California side of the Colorado in 1884, then ceded, apart from allotments, in a December 1893 agreement confirmed in August 1894.
Taken back in March 1884, when an executive order returned to the public domain what remained of three additions to the Great Sioux reservation east of the Missouri.
Set apart for the Turtle Mountain band of Chippewa in 1882; most of it was returned to the public domain by a March 1884 executive order.
Added to the Navaho reservation in 1884; this part, west of the 110th meridian in Utah, was returned to the public domain by a November 1892 order.
Townships of the 1882 Turtle Mountain Chippewa reserve that were kept when the rest was returned to the public domain in 1884; not ceded.
Set apart as the Chilocco reserve in Indian Territory by executive order in July 1884, for Indians educated at the Chilocco school; not a cession.
Townships once part of the Navaho reservation, returned to the public domain in 1884 and added back by an 1886 executive order; part of the reservation since.
Set apart as a reservation for the Northern Cheyenne in Montana by executive order in November 1884; not a cession.
Allotments to Sar-sarp-kin's band inside the former Columbia reservation, left out when the rest was returned to the public domain in 1886; they became individual property.
Added to the Duck Valley reserve in Idaho for Paddy Cap's band of Paiute by executive order in May 1886; not a cession.
Set up as a reservation for the Chehalis by executive order in October 1886, replacing their 1864 reserve; not a cession.
Held by Jemez Pueblo under a land grant from Spain in 1689, confirmed by the United States in 1858 and formally deeded in 1864: 17,510.45 acres. Land the pueblo holds, not a cession.
Held by Acoma Pueblo under a land grant from Spain in 1689, confirmed by the United States in 1858: 95,792 acres. Land the pueblo holds, not a cession.
Held by San Juan Pueblo under a land grant from Spain in 1689, confirmed by the United States in 1858 and formally deeded in 1864: 17,544.77 acres. Land the pueblo holds, not a cession.
Held by Picuris Pueblo under a land grant from Spain in 1689, confirmed by the United States in 1858 and formally deeded in 1864: 17,460.69 acres. Land the pueblo holds, not a cession.
Held by San Felipe Pueblo under a land grant from Spain in 1689, confirmed by the United States in 1858 and formally deeded in 1864: 34,766.86 acres. Land the pueblo holds, not a cession.
Held by Pecos Pueblo under a land grant from Spain in 1689, confirmed by the United States in 1858 and formally deeded in 1864: 18,763.33 acres. Land the pueblo holds, not a cession.
Held by Cochiti Pueblo under a land grant from Spain in 1689, confirmed by the United States in 1858 and formally deeded in 1864: 24,256.50 acres. Land the pueblo holds, not a cession.
Held by Santo Domingo Pueblo under a land grant from Spain in 1689, confirmed by the United States in 1858 and formally deeded in 1864: 74,743.11 acres. Land the pueblo holds, not a cession.
Held by Taos Pueblo under a land grant confirmed by the United States in 1858 and formally deeded in 1864: 17,360.65 acres. Land the pueblo holds, not a cession.
